newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England plans new bank regulatory system.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England plans new bank regulatory system.

text.p: The Bank of England on Monday proposed a new regulatory framework for the British banking industry which will take more account of individual risk situations and the controls present at individual banks.
It will mean that the Bank's inspectors will spend more time supervising banks judged to be running greater risks.

After the assessment the Bank will take action to remedy any problems found which could include improvements to systems and controls or even a requirement that the institution increase the capital it must hold relative to its assets.

The new framework follows a report commissioned by the Bank from consulting firm Arthur Andersen which followed criticism of the Bank's role in the collapse of British investment bank Barings in 1995.
Under the new framework, a business unit such as Barings Futures in Singapore, which lay at the heart of the Barings collapse, would be much more closely monitored.
The Bank will look closely at units which account for five percent or more of consolidated revenue, pre-tax profits or capital or are in some other way considered significant.

Banks will normally have their risk assessment done every year but, for those with higher risk profiles, the period will be cut to six months. It may be increased to every two years for those institutions with a low risk profile.

In its consultative paper, A Risk Based Approach to Supervision, the Bank proposes nine evaluation factors to assist in the systematic assessment of the business risk profile and to evaluate the adequacy of controls.
These will be capital; assets; market risk; earnings; liabilities; business; internal controls; organisation; and management.

The Bank says that pre-visit work will be essential to the success of the new framework but recognises that where significant units of a bank are supervised by overseas regulators, it may be difficult to obtain some information.
The Bank says it is already recruiting additional staff to cope with the increased workload.
The cost of supervision, which has been a source of concern to banks, will rise under the new regime for those banks with a higher risk profile and will fall for those with lower risk.
